title: Speech and Multimodal Systems
premise: Voice is the domain where the target employers live, and it is unusually unforgiving: a text product that takes two seconds is fine, and a voice product that takes two seconds is broken. Human conversation runs on a 300–500 ms response window, and most deployed voice agents sit at 1.4 seconds or worse. This course is about closing that gap and knowing exactly which hop to blame.
distinctive_asset: You are a native Mandarin and English bilingual living in Singapore. That makes you able to build something almost nobody in this field can: a real evaluation set for Singaporean-accented English and spontaneous Mandarin-English code-switching. Every off-the-shelf ASR system degrades on this and very few vendors can tell you by how much, because the data does not exist outside SEAME. Module 3 makes you build it and measure it. It is the most differentiated artifact in the whole programme, and the one most likely to start a conversation with a company selling voice into this region.
consent_note: M3.4 involves recording speech. Recording only yourself needs nothing. Recording anyone else requires their informed consent, and publishing a dataset of other people's voices requires explicit permission for that specific use — a voice is biometric data and consent to be recorded is not consent to be published. If consent is not clean, build the set from your own speech alone; the assignment is fully completable that way and the rubric does not reward volume.
advanced_standing_note: Advanced standing awarded 1 of 3 credits. Read Any Language and 1 Percent More Fluent already evidence synthesis integration at level 2 — live voice and model enumeration, quota handling, shipped. LearnIndo's speech-to-text path evidences ASR at level 1, which is 'touched it' and does not exempt anything. Nothing carries over for streaming, latency budgeting, quality measurement or turn-taking, which is most of the course.
laboratory: 1 Percent More Fluent and LearnIndo. Both already move audio in one direction; neither closes the loop, measures what it costs, or handles a user interrupting.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.measurement_note: Latency claims must carry a distribution measured from the user's action, not from an outbound API call. A mean alone fails the blocking check before any judge reads it.
panel.audio_handling: Judges receive transcripts and measurements, not raw audio. Where a claim depends on how something sounds, the submission must carry a listening protocol and its results rather than asking a judge to take it on trust.

items.brief: The best free treatment of the fundamentals that exists. Read before the papers, not after.
items.locator: The automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech chapter.

items.title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
whisper: the reference implementation
items.locator: whisper/ — decoding and the timestamp logic in particular.

items.title: Three systems, one voice
items.brief: Record two minutes of your own speech — one minute reading prepared text, one minute spontaneous — and transcribe it with three different ASR systems. Report word error rate for each against your own reference transcript. Note where the spontaneous minute diverges from the prepared one; that gap is the whole subject of this course.

items.title: Retention: ASR architectures and their assumptions
Common Voice: a massively multilingual speech corpus
Word error rate is not enough
items.brief: Build an ASR eval harness that reports WER, and then at least two measures that WER hides: entity error rate on names, numbers and codes, and error rate on the words that change meaning. Show a case where WER improves and your application gets worse. That case is the reason this assignment exists. Build it inside the eval suite from AIE-102 M6.4 rather than beside it — what is new here is the metrics, not the plumbing.

items.title: The errors that matter
items.brief: For one product, classify transcription errors by downstream consequence rather than by linguistic type: harmless, recoverable, and silently wrong. Report the distribution. The third category is the one that determines whether you can ship, and it is almost never measured.

items.title: Retention: recognition metrics and their blind spots
On the End-to-End Solution to Mandarin-English Code-switching Speech Recognition
items.brief: Built on SEAME — spontaneous Mandarin-English code-switching from Singaporean and Malaysian speakers. Your own linguistic environment, treated as a research problem.

items.title: CS-Dialogue: 104 hours of spontaneous code-switching dialogue
Build the eval set nobody has
items.brief: Construct an evaluation set of at least 60 utterances across three conditions: Singaporean-accented English, spontaneous Mandarin-English code-switching, and a monolingual control. Include the things that actually break systems here — particles, place names, mixed-language numerals, and terms that switch language mid-noun-phrase. Your own voice alone is sufficient; if you record anyone else, consent must be documented. Reference transcripts must state their own conventions, because how you transcribe a code-switch is a decision, not a fact.

items.title: Benchmark the vendors on it
items.brief: Run at least three commercial or open ASR systems against your set and report per-condition error rates. Then answer the question a buyer in this region would ask: which one would you recommend for a Singapore deployment, and what is the honest caveat? Report the degradation from control to code-switched as a ratio, because that number is the finding.

items.title: Retention: accent, code-switching and evaluation coverage
Text-to-speech chapters
items.locator: The text-to-speech sections of the speech chapter.

items.title: Neural codec language models for zero-shot TTS
Integrate synthesis properly
items.exempt_rationale: Read Any Language already does this in production: automatic language detection, live voice and model enumeration rather than hardcoded ids, instant previews and remaining-quota tracking. 1 Percent More Fluent adds language-appropriate narrator selection. Cite them.
items.brief: Integrate a synthesis provider with live voice and model enumeration, language-appropriate selection, and quota handling that degrades gracefully rather than failing at the worst moment.

items.title: Streaming synthesis
items.brief: Convert a non-streaming synthesis path in one of your products to stream, so audio starts before the text is complete. Measure time to first audio before and after, as the user experiences it. Then handle the case the naive version gets wrong: what happens when the upstream text stops mid-sentence.
checkpoints: time to first audio measured before and after

items.title: Voice quality is not one number
items.brief: Design a listening protocol for comparing two voices on your own content — what is played, in what order, to whom, and what they are asked. Run it, even if the panel is five people. Report the result and the protocol's weaknesses. A mean opinion score with no protocol is decoration.

items.title: WebRTC for the Curious
items.brief: Voice agents live or die on transport, and this is the only free text that explains why. Read at least the sections on jitter, packet loss and connection establishment.
items.locator: The chapters on connecting, media, and jitter and loss.

items.title: Understand and improve voice agent latency
items.brief: Vendor-authored, so read the numbers as a floor rather than a promise. The decomposition by hop is the right one.

items.title: Where the milliseconds actually go
items.brief: Build a full loop — microphone to recognition to model to synthesis to speaker — and instrument every hop. Report the budget as a distribution per hop, measured from the user's action. Then state which single hop you would attack first and what it would cost. Most people discover the model is not the problem.
checkpoints: per-hop distributions and an attack plan

items.title: The transport experiment
items.brief: Degrade the network deliberately — added latency, jitter, packet loss — and report what your loop does at each level. State the conditions under which it becomes unusable, in terms a customer could check against their own office wifi.

items.title: Retention: transport, jitter and their latency effects
Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue
items.brief: Full-duplex: the model listens while it speaks. The clearest argument that turn-taking is architectural rather than a feature you bolt on.

items.title: Barge-in that works
items.brief: Make your loop interruptible: the user speaks over the agent, the agent stops promptly, and the conversation continues coherently from where it was cut. Measure stop latency from the onset of user speech. Then handle the hard half — distinguishing a genuine interruption from a cough, a background voice, or the user saying 'mm-hm' while agreeing.

items.title: The awkward pause
items.brief: Find the endpointing threshold where your agent starts talking over people, and the one where it feels sluggish. Report both numbers and what you chose. Then say how the right answer differs for a Mandarin speaker, an English speaker, and someone switching between them mid-sentence — because it does, and it is the kind of thing a regional deployment gets wrong.

items.title: Retention: endpointing, barge-in and duplex behaviour
Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision
Beat your own PDF extractor
items.brief: Career Side Quests reads CVs by finding column gutters and reading inside each one — a solution you built by hand after two-column layouts spliced a sidebar label into someone's work history. Now attack the same problem with a vision-language model reading the page as an image. Build a labelled set of at least 25 real CVs and postings, including the two-column ones that broke the original, and measure both approaches on extraction accuracy, cost per document and latency. Report which wins and on which documents — the answer is very unlikely to be uniform.

items.title: Structured extraction that fails closed
items.brief: A vision model reading a document will invent a field it cannot see, and a plausible invented salary is worse than a missing one. Apply AIE-101's schema discipline and AIE-102's verbatim-check discipline to visual extraction: every extracted value must be locatable on the page, and anything that cannot be located is discarded rather than returned. Report the rejection rate and what it catches.

items.title: Where vision is the wrong tool
items.brief: Name the document types where your text pipeline should stay, and say why using your own numbers. Cost, latency and accuracy all matter here, and the fashionable answer is frequently the wrong one.

items.title: Retention: vision-language models and document extraction
Ship a voice loop
items.brief: Put a working voice interaction into one of your products, publicly reachable — LearnIndo's spoken exercises are the obvious home. Streaming in both directions, interruptible, with a measured end-to-end budget.

items.title: The latency and accuracy report
items.brief: Publish the per-hop latency budget, the code-switching benchmark from M3.5, the barge-in numbers, and what you could not fix. The code-switching results are the part a reader will not have seen anywhere else — lead with them.

items.title: Publish
items.brief: Publish this as the next chapter of your public engineering log — one growing site, not a sixth standalone post. The chapter must stand alone on its own page for a reader arriving cold, and must connect backwards to at least one result from an earlier chapter. Publish at a stable public URL. Release the code-switching evaluation set if and only if consent permits it; otherwise publish the methodology and the results without the audio.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your report at defense time, answered aloud without notes. Fitting, for this course, that the defense is itself a speech interface. Questions are drawn from both halves of the course — a defense of a speech-and-multimodal course that never asks about documents leaves half of what it certifies untested.
sample_question_shapes: A customer in Singapore asks whether your recommended ASR will work for their support line. Answer from your own numbers.
Your p95 end-to-end is X. Which hop, and what would you have to give up to fix it?
Your barge-in triggers on background speech. Talk me through the trade you made and who it hurts.
You found a case where the vision model lost to your old extractor. Why, and would that still hold on a different document set?

completion.required: All non-exempt assignments and the project submitted. Exempted items are satisfied by citing the existing artifact and are recorded as advanced standing, not as coursework.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the five speech skills. FSRS then decays them, so the transcript reports what is currently held.

multimodal_note: Multimodal here means documents, not general vision. Image classification and object detection are a different specialisation and are not on the path to the target roles. Document understanding is, because 'can it read our contracts?' is one of the most common enterprise questions there is — and because Career Side Quests already solves a version of it by hand, which gives this module a baseline to beat rather than a toy to build.
